title: Testing for alkenes with bromine water
keyIdea: Shake a few drops of orange bromine water with a liquid. If the orange turns colourless, the liquid has a C=C bond: bromine adds across it and is used up, so the compound is unsaturated. If it stays orange, there is no C=C. Each C=C uses up the same amount of bromine, so more bromine decolourised means more C=C.

kid: Bromine water is a see-through orange liquid. Add a few drops to a test tube of something, put a bung in and shake.
If the orange goes away and the tube looks colourless, there is a carbon to carbon double bond inside. The bromine joins on at the double bond, so it is used up.
If the tube stays orange, there is no double bond. Hexane stays orange. So does cyclohexane, even though its formula is the same as hexene's.
Keep adding drops and the colour keeps going, until all the double bonds have been used. Something with more double bonds can take more drops.
adult: Bromine water is a weak orange solution of bromine. Shake it with an alkene at room temperature and it turns from orange to colourless in seconds. The C=C opens and a bromine atom bonds to one of its carbons. With pure bromine the product is a dibromoalkane, such as 1,2-dibromoethane. In bromine water, water joins in too, and the main product is a bromoalcohol. Either way, the bromine is used up and the colour goes.

An alkane has only single bonds, so nothing can add on and the bromine water stays orange. Test a known alkane next to the unknown as a control: then you know the colour loss came from a C=C and not from mixing.

Because each C=C reacts with one Br₂, the test can compare unsaturation. Equal amounts of hexa-1,5-diene (two C=C per molecule) decolourise twice as much bromine water as hex-1-ene. Vegetable oils such as sunflower oil decolourise more than butter, so they are more unsaturated.

Common mistakes: writing 'orange to clear' (clear means see-through, which bromine water already is; say colourless); swapping the two results; deciding a CₙH₂ₙ compound must be an alkene, when cyclohexane has that formula and no C=C; thinking the test tells you which alkene it is; and saying alkanes react the same way. In bright sunlight alkanes do react, very slowly, by swapping H for Br. That is a different reaction.

familyTip: Find the nutrition labels on a bottle of sunflower oil and a pack of butter. Compare the 'saturates' line with the total fat. Which one has more unsaturated fat, the kind with C=C bonds? That is the one that would decolourise more bromine water.

worked.title: Three colourless liquids are hexane, hex-1-ene and cyclohexane. Plan a test to find the alkene.
steps: Put the same small amount of each liquid in its own test tube.
Add a few drops of bromine water to each, put in a bung and shake.
Hex-1-ene turns the bromine water from orange to colourless: it has a C=C.
Hexane and cyclohexane both stay orange. Cyclohexane is C₆H₁₂ like hex-1-ene, but its six carbons form a ring of single bonds, so it is saturated.

practice.prompt: Equal amounts are tested. Hex-1-ene uses up {a} drops of bromine water before the orange stays. A compound with {n} C=C bonds in each molecule is tested the same way. How many drops does it use up?
practice.hint: Each C=C uses up the same amount of bromine. {n} C=C per molecule means {n} times as much.
practice.explain: One C=C per molecule used {a} drops, so {n} per molecule use {n} × {a} = {=a*n} drops.

practice.prompt: Equal amounts of two oils are tested. Oil P uses up {p} drops of bromine water. Oil Q uses up {=p*k} drops. How many times as many C=C bonds does Q have?
practice.hint: Drops used up are in proportion to the number of C=C bonds. Divide {=p*k} by {p}.
practice.explain: {=p*k} ÷ {p} = {k}, so oil Q has {k} times as many C=C bonds. It is the more unsaturated oil.

practice.prompt: How should you describe a positive result for the bromine water test?
choices: Orange to colourless
Orange to clear
Colourless to orange
practice.hint: Bromine water is already see-through. What happens to its colour?
practice.explain: The orange colour disappears, so the change is orange to colourless. Clear means see-through, which it was all along.

practice.prompt: Cyclohexane, C₆H₁₂, has the same formula as hex-1-ene. What happens when it is shaken with bromine water?
choices: It stays orange, because its ring has only single bonds
It turns colourless, because it is C₆H₁₂
It turns colourless slowly, because it is a ring
practice.hint: The test looks for a C=C bond, not a formula.
practice.explain: Cyclohexane is saturated: six carbons joined in a ring by single bonds. With no C=C, the bromine has nothing to add to and stays orange.

practice.prompt: Why test hexane next to the unknown liquid?
choices: As a control: it shows that a liquid with no C=C leaves the colour orange
To make the bromine water more orange
Because hexane reacts faster than alkenes
practice.hint: What would you compare the unknown's result with?
practice.explain: Hexane has no C=C, so it stays orange. If the unknown turns colourless and the hexane does not, the change is down to a C=C.

pool.prompt: Liquid X turns bromine water from orange to colourless. What does this show?
choices: X contains a C=C bond, so it is unsaturated
X is saturated
X must be ethene
pool.hint: What does bromine need in order to add on?
pool.explain: Decolourising bromine water shows a C=C is present: X is unsaturated. Every alkene gives this result, so it cannot say which one X is.

pool.prompt: Liquid Y is C₅H₁₀ but leaves bromine water orange. What is Y most likely to be?
choices: Cyclopentane, a ring with no C=C
Pentene, because it fits CₙH₂ₙ
Pentane, because it has five carbons
pool.hint: Which CₙH₂ₙ compounds have no double bond?
pool.explain: C₅H₁₀ fits both pentene and cyclopentane. Staying orange rules out a C=C, so Y is the ring. Pentane is C₅H₁₂, so it does not fit.

pool.prompt: Equal amounts are tested. A diene, with two C=C per molecule, uses up {=2*a} drops of bromine water. How many drops does an alkene with one C=C per molecule use up?
pool.hint: Half as many C=C bonds use up half as much bromine.
pool.explain: {=2*a} ÷ 2 = {a} drops. Each C=C takes the same amount of bromine.

pool.prompt: A sample of cyclohexene can use up {c} drops of bromine water. {b} drops are added and the tube is shaken. How many drops' worth of bromine are left to colour the tube orange?
pool.hint: The first {c} drops are used up by the C=C bonds. What is left over?
pool.explain: {b} − {c} = {=b-c} drops' worth is left over, so the tube stays orange. The C=C bonds have all reacted.

pool.prompt: Why does bromine water lose its colour when shaken with an alkene?
choices: Bromine adds across the C=C and is used up
The alkene dilutes the colour until you cannot see it
Bromine swaps places with hydrogen atoms, as it does with any hydrocarbon
pool.hint: Hexane added the same way leaves the colour. What is different about an alkene?
pool.explain: The C=C opens and bromine bonds to its carbons. The orange bromine is used up. Dilution cannot be the reason, because hexane stays orange.

pool.prompt: Which of these will decolourise bromine water?
choices: Propene, CH₂=CHCH₃
Propane, CH₃CH₂CH₃
Cyclopropane, a ring of three carbons with single bonds
pool.hint: Check each formula for a double bond between two carbons.
pool.explain: Only propene has a C=C, so only propene decolourises bromine water. Propane and cyclopropane have single bonds only.

pool.prompt: Equal amounts of sunflower oil, olive oil and butter are tested. They use up 5, 3 and 1 drops of bromine water. Which is the most unsaturated?
choices: Sunflower oil
Butter
They are all equally unsaturated
pool.hint: More drops used up means more C=C bonds.
pool.explain: Sunflower oil used up the most bromine, so it has the most C=C bonds. Butter has the fewest, so it is the most saturated of the three.

pool.prompt: Hexane and bromine water are left on a sunny windowsill for hours, and the colour slowly fades. Does this show hexane is an alkene?
choices: No: in strong light alkanes slowly swap H for Br, a different reaction from the quick alkene test
Yes: any colour loss means a C=C
Yes: hexane is an alkene
pool.hint: How fast does an alkene decolourise bromine water, and does it need light?
pool.explain: Alkenes decolourise bromine water in seconds, light or not. The slow fading with hexane is substitution caused by light. That is why the test is done quickly.

visual.caption: What does each one do to bromine water? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Cyclohexene, a ring with one C=C
